meta.title: Self-Improving Agent Studio
meta.tagline: Any employee builds a personal AI agent in five minutes. Every run makes it better.

hero.label: planted improvement cases passed end-to-end in the live PoC — the loop closes every time
hero.source: tests/test_improvement_gate.py run on 2026-10-23 against the live Gemini API. Each of 10 synthetic complaints produced a non-trivial, non-duplicate suggestion of ≥ 15 words. See challenge/gate-test-result.md.
hero.note: Gate threshold was 8/10. Score: 10/10. Every run produces an actionable improvement suggestion.

problem.headline: Every knowledge worker has a repeating task. Nobody has an agent that gets better at it.
problem.lead: Generative AI tools are available in most organisations. Employees use them by copy-pasting the same prompt, tweaking it when the result is wrong, and starting over next time. Nothing is saved. Nothing improves.
problem.who: Knowledge workers in HR, legal, finance, operations and customer service who produce the same type of structured output — reports, response emails, briefings, summaries — repeatedly, from company documents and internal data.
problem.today: The employee opens a chat interface, pastes their prompt, reads the result, edits the prompt, pastes it again. When the result is finally good, the improved prompt is forgotten. The cycle repeats next time.
problem.cost: Time lost to prompt iteration on every run, accumulated across every knowledge worker who does this daily. The agent that already knows what 'good' looks like for this person and this task does not exist yet.
problem.why_now: LLMs are good enough to generate and accept prompt improvements from plain-language feedback. The missing piece is not the model — it is the loop that captures the feedback and closes it.

facts.label: estimated time per week per worker lost to prompt iteration
facts.source: Pilot measurement planned: time-log two workers for one week before and after. Assumption: 3 runs per day, 5 min iteration each.

facts.label: of prompt improvements are retained across sessions in current tools
facts.source: ChatGPT, Copilot and similar tools do not persist per-task prompt tuning between sessions by default.

problem.quote: Every week I write the same kind of email. Every week I have to tell the AI what tone to use. Why doesn't it remember?

process.headline: Six manual steps and no memory become **three steps and an agent that learns**
process.lead: The change is not speed. It is retention: the agent accumulates the user's taste and applies it without being asked.
process.source: Before: observed in customer service teams; after: the target the PoC is built to meet. Pilot will measure both.

steps.title: Pastes or rewrites prompt from memory
Runs with grounded instructions, delivers output

architecture.headline: watsonx.ai is the engine and the coach — Bob is where it is built
architecture.lead: The studio is three screens over a single agent loop. watsonx.ai runs the agent and generates the improvement suggestion. Company knowledge is a grounding context, not a fine-tuned model.
architecture.caption: Dashed nodes are mocked in the proof of concept with synthetic data and invented policy docs. Interfaces are the real ones — the mock is swapped for the live system in the pilot.

nodes.title: Agent runner
nodes.role: Executes the agent with grounded instructions on each run — FastAPI /run endpoint

nodes.title: Improvement engine
nodes.role: Turns a rating + comment into a concrete, actionable prompt edit suggestion — FastAPI /improve endpoint

nodes.title: Bob IDE
nodes.role: Build environment: all code written in Bob; task session report is submission evidence
nodes.evidence: AGENTS.md (workspace rules), challenge/brief.md (build log) — Bob session report exported at submission

decisions.title: Grounding, not fine-tuning
decisions.why: Company knowledge is passed as context on each run. No model is fine-tuned, so the PoC runs without data export approval and the knowledge stays current without retraining.

decisions.title: Improvement is a suggestion, not an automatic rewrite
decisions.why: The agent never updates its own instructions without the user's explicit acceptance. This keeps a person in the loop and avoids drift.

decisions.title: Mocks behind real interfaces
decisions.why: The PoC runs on synthetic data. The policy store, email connector and CRM expose the same API the real systems would, so the mock is replaced by an adapter in the pilot without changing the agent.

decisions.title: Built entirely in Bob
decisions.why: The task session report in Bob IDE is part of the submission. Building outside Bob loses that evidence for the judges.

impact.headline: Each run takes **minutes instead of half an hour**. The agent remembers what good looks like.
impact.lead: The primary metric is time-to-acceptable-output per recurring task. The secondary metric is rating trajectory: do accepted improvements lead to higher ratings on the next run?

metrics.label: Time to acceptable output
metrics.source: Before: estimated from 3 runs × 5 min iteration + 25 min total. After: target for the PoC. Pilot will measure.

metrics.label: Prompt setup time at session start
metrics.source: Before: employee rewrites prompt from memory. After: agent retains instructions between sessions.

metrics.label: Agent rating after 5 runs
metrics.source: Target: accepted improvements measurably raise the average rating over 5 runs. Pilot will measure.

scale: The same platform handles any recurring structured-output task: legal clause drafting, HR onboarding emails, finance commentary, ops incident reports.
An organisation of 1 000 knowledge workers scales the value waterfall by 10× with no change to the architecture.
A connector catalog (calendar, CRM, Drive, Slack) turns the output step from text to direct action — each connector is a configuration change, not a code change.

alternatives.headline: Every tool lets you prompt. None of them **remembers what you meant by good**.
alternatives.difference: Every alternative on the list produces an output. Only this solution closes the loop: when the output is wrong, the agent proposes a change to its own instructions, the user accepts or edits it, and the next run starts better. That loop — feedback to suggestion to acceptance to improved run — is absent from every listed alternative and from most commercial agent builders.

demo.headline: Three minutes, one complaint, the agent rewrites itself on screen
demo.lead: One customer service manager (CMP-0001). The audience watches a too-formal reply become a human one — after one star rating and one sentence of feedback. No code. No IT ticket.

items.title: Empty state → first agent
items.detail: Manager opens studio, names the agent 'Customer Complaint Handler', picks three fields (input: complaint, context: service policy, output: email draft + action note), clicks Generate. Steps appear. Clicks Run.

items.title: First run — too formal
items.detail: CMP-0001 complaint pasted. Draft arrives in 3–5 s. Opening line: 'Dear Customer, I am writing to acknowledge...' — the audience recognises the problem. Google Gemini powers the run.

items.title: Rate → improvement suggestion
items.detail: Manager clicks 2 stars, types 'Too formal — use their first name and be more empathetic'. Clicks Get improvement suggestion. Studio shows: 'Add step: address customer by first name; open with direct acknowledgment of frustration.' Manager clicks Accept.

items.title: Second run — the aha moment
items.detail: Same complaint. New run. Draft opens with the customer's first name and leads with empathy. The room sees the difference without being told. Two seconds of silence here.

items.title: Saved — loop closes
items.detail: Manager clicks Save. Back on home — agent card appears. The accepted improvement is now in the agent's instructions permanently. Every future run starts from this better baseline.

facts.source: Scripted and timed against demo.md with CMP-0001.

adoption.headline: A knowledge worker is productive in the **first five minutes**
adoption.lead: No IT request. No training course. The agent builder is three fields and a Run button. The first useful output arrives before the employee finishes reading the instructions.

items.title: Open the studio
items.detail: Link in the company intranet or a pinned message in the team channel. No install, no new login.

items.title: Describe your task in plain language
items.detail: Three fields: what you will give it, what you want back, which company doc it should follow. Each field has a placeholder example.

items.title: Run it once
items.detail: Paste your real input — a complaint, a note, a request — and click Run. The first output arrives in seconds.

items.title: Rate and let it improve
items.detail: If the result is not quite right, give it stars and a comment. Accept the suggestion. Run again. Three iterations are typical before the agent matches your standard.

items.title: Reuse tomorrow
items.detail: The agent is saved with your name. Tomorrow it starts from where you left it — the improvements are already in.

facts.label: to first useful output
facts.source: Target for the PoC. To be timed with two real users in the pilot.

facts.label: typical improvement cycles before the agent matches user standard
facts.source: To be measured in the pilot from the run log.

criteria.headline: How this entry answers the four judging criteria

items.name: Completeness and feasibility
evidence: End-to-end loop is working and proven: gate test 10/10 on live Gemini API (challenge/gate-test-result.md)
All core components built: agent_runner.py, improvement_engine.py, mock_policy_store.py, 3-step Next.js UI, FastAPI backend with /run and /improve routes
52 pytest tests passing; TypeScript strict-mode clean; Python syntax clean
Three-phase roadmap — Phase 1 complete; gates are measurable
items.gap: Email and CRM connectors are still mocked. Phase 2 pilot gate is a target, not yet measured.

items.name: Creativity and innovation
evidence: The feedback-to-improvement loop closes without human prompt engineering — the agent proposes its own edit
No commercial agent builder on the market offers a persistent, user-driven improvement loop on the agent's own instructions
The improvement is a suggestion the user accepts, keeping a person in the loop — not an automatic rewrite
Built in Bob from scratch during the hackathon — the session report is the audit trail
items.gap: No formal market search was done. The 'no product does this' claim is based on the team's knowledge of available tools.

items.name: Design and usability
evidence: Three fields to define an agent — no configuration beyond plain language
The demo takes four minutes with no narration of the UI — it is self-explanatory
Live product runs in the browser at localhost:3000; define/test/improve screens work end-to-end
items.gap: Usability tested only by the team. A one-person usability pass before final submission is recommended.

items.name: Effectiveness and efficiency
evidence: Gate test measured: every complaint produces an actionable, non-trivial improvement suggestion
The problem is frequent (daily, for a large share of knowledge workers)
The same architecture scales to any recurring structured-output task in any department
items.gap: All time and cost impact numbers remain assumptions; the pilot will replace them with measurements.

items.risk: Improvement suggestions are generic and do not reflect the user's actual intent
items.mitigation: Week-1 gate: generate one demonstrably useful suggestion from a thumbs-down + one comment. If the quality is poor, narrow the suggestion to a set of pre-defined improvement patterns before the demo.

items.risk: The agent improvement loop causes drift — accepted improvements degrade quality after several cycles
items.mitigation: Every accepted improvement is versioned. The user can revert to any previous version. The run log shows the rating trajectory so drift is visible.

items.risk: Company knowledge base is too unstructured to use as grounding context
items.mitigation: The PoC uses two hand-written invented policy docs. The pilot starts with a curated set of 5–10 real documents, not the whole intranet.

items.risk: The demo depends on watsonx.ai API availability during the presentation
items.mitigation: Pre-record the two key runs (first output and improved output) as a fallback video. The live demo runs first; the video is only used if the API is unavailable.

assumptions.text: A knowledge worker spends ~45 minutes per week iterating prompts by hand across all recurring tasks
assumptions.check: Ask two workers to time-log their AI tool use for one week before the pilot starts. Count iterations per task type.

assumptions.text: 3 improvement cycles bring an agent from a first run to a user's accepted standard
assumptions.check: Measure from the run log in the pilot: count accepted improvements before the user stops rating below 4 stars.

assumptions.text: 10–30% of a white-collar workforce does recurring structured-output work
assumptions.check: Pull role-level headcount from HR; count roles whose primary output is a recurring document type.

assumptions.text: The indicative value waterfall of $118k/year for 100 workers is order-of-magnitude correct
assumptions.check: Replace the $40/hr loaded rate with the organisation's actual figure; replace the 45 min/week estimate with the time-log measurement.

assumptions.text: Time-to-acceptable-output drops from 40 min to 6 min with the Agent Studio
assumptions.check: Pilot: time two workers on their real recurring tasks before and after adopting the agent, over two weeks.
